chart.exploreHint: Drag to move around; + and − zoom, the last button resets the view.
view.label: Views
variable.notFound: This column doesn't exist in the dataset.
variable.excluded: This column is excluded from analyses. Include it again on the Columns page.
variable.ignored: Ignored column: there is nothing to analyse.
variable.sampleNote: Drawn from a reproducible sample of {sample} of {n} values.
variable.qqNote: Points on the line = normal. Curving away at the ends = heavier or lighter tails than a normal.
explain.rows: Every row of the dataset, including those where this column is empty.
explain.count: Rows with a usable number (not empty, not infinite). Every statistic below is computed on these.
explain.missing: Empty cells, or text that couldn't be read as a number.
explain.infinite: Values equal to +∞ or −∞. They are left out of the statistics.
explain.zeros: Values exactly equal to 0. Many zeros can mean 'not applicable' was coded as 0.
explain.negatives: Values below 0. Check they make sense for this measure (a negative age is an error).
explain.mean: The average: sum of the values divided by their count. Pulled toward extreme values.
explain.std: Typical distance from the mean (sample standard deviation). Same unit as the data.
explain.cv: Standard deviation divided by the mean: spread relative to size, without unit. Above 1 = very dispersed.
explain.p1: 1% of the values are below this one.
explain.p5: 5% of the values are below this one.
explain.p10: 10% of the values are below this one.
explain.q1: First quartile: a quarter of the values are below.
explain.median: The middle value: half below, half above. Robust to extreme values, unlike the mean.
explain.q3: Third quartile: three quarters of the values are below.
explain.p90: 90% of the values are below this one.
explain.p95: 95% of the values are below this one.
explain.p99: 99% of the values are below this one.
explain.iqr: Interquartile range, Q3 − Q1: the width of the middle half of the data. Robust to outliers.
explain.mad: Median absolute deviation: median of the distances to the median. A robust alternative to the standard deviation.
explain.skewness: Asymmetry. 0 = symmetric; > 0 = long tail to the right (a few large values); < 0 = long tail to the left. Beyond ±1, strongly skewed.
explain.kurtosis: Tail weight compared with a normal distribution (which scores 0). > 0 = more extreme values than a normal; < 0 = fewer.
normality.summary: {rejected} of {total} tests reject normality at α = {alpha}.
normality.summaryNone: No test rejects normality at α = {alpha}.
normality.large: With n = {n}, even tiny departures from normality are detected: look at the QQ-plot to judge whether they matter in practice.
normality.sample: Tests ran on a reproducible sample of {sample} of the {n} values.
normality.intro: Each test asks: could these values come from a normal (bell-shaped) distribution? A p-value below α means the data is unlikely under normality.
test.shapiro.name: Shapiro–Wilk
test.shapiro.detail: Compares the sorted values with the ones a normal distribution would give. The most powerful general test for small and medium samples; reliable up to 5,000 values.
test.dagostino.name: D'Agostino–Pearson K²
test.dagostino.detail: Combines skewness and kurtosis into one statistic: it rejects when the data is too asymmetric or its tails too heavy or too light. Needs at least 20 values.
test.anderson.name: Anderson–Darling
test.anderson.detail: Measures the distance between the empirical and normal distribution functions, giving extra weight to the tails. Good at spotting extreme values a normal wouldn't produce.
test.jarque_bera.name: Jarque–Bera
test.jarque_bera.detail: Checks whether skewness and kurtosis match a normal's (0 and 0). Common in econometrics; best with large samples.
test.lilliefors.name: Lilliefors (Kolmogorov–Smirnov)
test.lilliefors.detail: The largest gap between the empirical distribution and a normal with the same mean and standard deviation. The correct version of KS when those are estimated from the data.
fit.title: Candidate laws
fit.bestLog: A log transformation would bring it close to normal.
fit.sample: Laws fitted by maximum likelihood on a reproducible sample of {n} values.
fit.explainAic: Akaike information criterion: how well the law fits, penalised by its number of parameters. Lower is better; only differences matter (> 10 = clearly better).
fit.explainBic: Bayesian information criterion: like AIC with a stronger penalty for parameters on large samples.
fit.explainKs: Largest gap between the empirical and fitted cumulative distributions (0 = perfect).
fit.transformsHint: Preview only: the data itself is never modified.
outliers.explain.iqr: Tukey's rule: below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. The box plot's whiskers.
outliers.explain.iqr3: Tukey's 'far out' rule: beyond 3 × IQR from the quartiles. Only the most extreme values.
outliers.explain.zscore: More than 3 standard deviations from the mean. Assumes a roughly normal shape, and outliers inflate the deviation itself.
outliers.explain.robust: Modified z-score of Iglewicz & Hoaglin: distance to the median in MADs, above 3.5. Not fooled by the outliers it looks for.
outliers.none: No value is flagged by this rule.
cat.imbalance: "{label}" alone makes up {share} of the rows: models and averages will be dominated by it.
cat.explainEntropy: Shannon entropy in bits: the average surprise of drawing a category. 0 = always the same; log2(k) = all k categories equally frequent.
cat.explainEvenness: Entropy divided by its maximum: 1 = perfectly even categories, near 0 = one category dominates.
cat.explainHerfindahl: Sum of squared shares: the chance two random rows share a category. 1/k = even, 1 = a single category.
date.noGaps: No empty period: the series is continuous at this step.
id.allUnique: Every value is unique: a valid key.
filters.hint: Filter the rows of every page (F)
filters.title: Filters
filters.logic: Filters combine with AND; checked values with OR.
filters.tooManyValues: Too many distinct values to list: use “contains” or “equals”.
filters.showChips: Show active filters under the top bar
filters.emptyBody: Loosen or remove a filter to see data again.
filters.filteredNote: Computed on the {rows} rows that pass the filters.
filters.columnsNote: Summaries describe the {rows} filtered rows; detected types always use every row.
compare.title: Compare
compare.description: Cross two variables: the chart and the statistical test follow their types. Add a third numeric for 3D, or a category for color.
compare.pick: Pick an X and a Y column to compare them.
compare.noTest: No test applies to this pair.
compare.alphaNote: Significant = p < 0.05. Effect size says whether the relationship matters in practice; with many rows, even tiny effects become significant.
compare.densityNote: Counts of rows per cell, over every row (not a sample).
compare.sampleNote: Drawn from a reproducible sample of {sample} of {rows} rows; statistics use every row.
btest.pearson.detail: Strength of the straight-line relationship, from −1 to 1, on every row. Sensitive to outliers; assumes a roughly linear link.
btest.spearman.detail: Correlation of the ranks: catches any monotonic relationship (always rising or always falling), robust to outliers.
btest.kendall.detail: Share of pairs of rows ordered the same way on both variables, minus those ordered oppositely. Robust; smaller values than Spearman for the same strength.
btest.welch_t.detail: Compares the means of two groups without assuming equal variances. Effect: Cohen's d, the gap in standard deviations (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large).
btest.mann_whitney.detail: Rank-based alternative to the t-test: do values of one group tend to be larger? No normality assumption. Effect: rank-biserial correlation.
btest.anova.detail: Compares the means of 3 or more groups, assuming equal variances. Effect: η², the share of variance explained by the groups (0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large).
btest.welch_anova.detail: ANOVA that does not assume equal variances: the safer choice when groups spread differently.
btest.kruskal.detail: Rank-based alternative to ANOVA: do some groups tend to have larger values? No normality assumption. Effect: ε².
btest.levene.detail: Checks whether the groups have the same spread (median-centred, robust). It decides between classic and Welch's ANOVA.
btest.chi2.detail: Are the two categories independent? Compares observed counts with those expected if they were unrelated. Effect: Cramér's V, from 0 (none) to 1 (perfect).
btest.fisher.detail: Exact p-value for 2 × 2 tables, reliable even with small counts. Statistic: the odds ratio.
btest.found.difference.no: No evidence that the groups differ
correlations.title: Correlations
correlations.description: How every pair of variables is linked, whatever their types, and what deserves your attention.
correlations.sampled: Computed on a reproducible sample of {rows} of {total} rows
correlations.tooFew: Pick at least two numeric or category columns.
correlations.legend: Blue = positive, red = negative (numeric pairs only); categories use Cramér's V and η, from 0 to 1. Click a cell to compare the two variables.
correlations.truncated: {count} more columns beyond the 60-column limit: choose the columns to include.
insights.title: Insights
insights.none: Nothing stands out: no strong link, skew, imbalance or missing values.
correlations.focusHint: what relates to it, best evidence first
correlations.pairsHint: Best evidence first. adj. p = p-value adjusted for testing every pair at once.
evidence.title: Evidence
evidence.strongHint: Large effect, very unlikely to be chance (adj. p < 0.001).
evidence.moderateHint: At least a medium effect, statistically significant (adj. p < 0.05).
evidence.weakHint: Either a small but real effect, or a notable effect that could be chance (adj. p ≥ 0.05).
evidence.noneHint: Negligible effect, or small and not significant.
evidence.showLabel: Links to show, by level of evidence
data.title: Data
data.description: The rows behind every chart, after your filters: check them, search them, export them.
data.invalid: "{value}" cannot be read in this column's type: shown as stored.
data.exportRows: The {rows} rows shown (filters, mode, search, sort)
data.noDuplicates: No duplicate rows: every row is unique.
data.noMissing: No row has a missing value.
filters.duplicatesHint: Rows whose value of {column} appears more than once.
filters.keyUniqueHint: One row per combination of {key} (like a primary key).
filters.keyDuplicatesHint: Rows whose combination of {key} appears more than once.
filters.needKeyColumns: Tick at least one more column for the key.
settings.motionHint: Reduce cuts transitions; System follows your OS accessibility setting.
settings.analysisIntro: Starting values for datasets you haven't customised yet; each page can still change them.
settings.topNHint: Categories shown on Overview cards; the rest is grouped as Others.
settings.pageSizeHint: Variables shown per page on the Overview.
settings.alphaHint: Significance level: a p-value below α means "probably not normal".
settings.detectionIntro: Applied to the next detections (imports and "Re-run detection" on the Columns page). Validated types and manual corrections are kept.
settings.discreteMaxHint: Whole numbers with at most this many distinct values are discrete (shown as bars).
settings.parseRateHint: Share of the values that must read as numbers or dates to convert a text column.
settings.identifierUniqueHint: Share of distinct values above which a text column is an identifier.
settings.emptyRateHint: Share of empty values above which a column is ignored.

btest.mann_kendall.detail: Counts, over every pair of periods, how often the later value is higher than the earlier one. It detects a steady rise or fall of any shape, is robust to outliers, and is computed on one aggregated value per period. tau runs from -1 (always falls) to 1 (always rises).
time.coarsened: Shown per {period} to keep the series readable.
time.trend.none: No clear trend over the period.
time.trend.perYear: About {pct} % per year relative to its average level.
time.trend.autocorrelated: Successive values are strongly linked (a cycle or a slow drift), so the p-value is optimistic. The Time series page tests this properly.
time.partial.both: The first and last {period} are incomplete: they are drawn but left out of the trend test.
time.partial.first: The first {period} is incomplete: it is drawn but left out of the trend test.
time.partial.last: The last {period} is incomplete: it is drawn but left out of the trend test.
time.bandSingle: The band is drawn for a single series only
tsm.mann_kendall.what: Counts, over every pair of periods, how often the later value is higher. Robust to outliers and to the shape of the trend.
tsm.mann_kendall.no: No evidence of a monotonic trend.
tsm.sen.what: Median of the slopes between every pair of periods: the typical change per period, with its 95 % interval.
tsm.sen.h0: Not a test: the trend is clear when the interval excludes 0.
tsm.sen.yes: The slope interval excludes 0: the series changes steadily.
tsm.sen.no: The slope interval includes 0: no clear change per period.
tsm.hamed_rao.what: Mann-Kendall with its variance corrected for autocorrelation: honest when successive values are linked.
tsm.hamed_rao.h0: H0: no monotonic trend, allowing for autocorrelation.
tsm.hamed_rao.yes: A trend remains once autocorrelation is allowed for.
tsm.hamed_rao.no: No trend once autocorrelation is allowed for.
tsm.seasonal_mk.what: Mann-Kendall within each position of the cycle (each month…), summed: a trend the seasonal pattern cannot fake.
tsm.seasonal_mk.h0: H0: no monotonic trend in any season.
tsm.seasonal_mk.yes: A trend runs through the seasons.
tsm.cox_stuart.what: Compares each value of the first half with its counterpart in the second half (a sign test).
tsm.cox_stuart.yes: The second half is consistently higher or lower.
tsm.cox_stuart.no: No consistent difference between the halves.
tsm.spearman_time.what: Rank correlation between the value and time.
tsm.spearman_time.h0: H0: no monotonic association with time.
tsm.spearman_time.yes: The value is associated with time.
tsm.linear_trend.what: A straight line through the series: slope, t-test and R².
tsm.linear_trend.no: The straight-line slope does not differ from 0.
tsm.kruskal_season.what: Compares the positions of the cycle (each weekday, each month…) once the trend is removed. ε² measures how much they differ.
tsm.kruskal_season.h0: H0: every position of the cycle has the same level.
tsm.kruskal_season.yes: The positions of the cycle differ: there is seasonality.
tsm.kruskal_season.no: No evidence that the positions of the cycle differ.
tsm.periodogram.what: Splits the variance into cycles of every length and reports the strongest ones.
tsm.periodogram.h0: Not a test: shows the dominant cycle length.
tsm.friedman.what: Kruskal–Wallis paired by cycle: each full cycle is a block, which removes slow level changes.
tsm.friedman.h0: H0: every position of the cycle has the same level.
tsm.friedman.yes: The positions of the cycle differ within cycles.
tsm.qs.what: Positive autocorrelation one and two cycles apart on the differenced series (the test used by X-13ARIMA-SEATS).
tsm.fisher_g.what: Is the strongest cycle in the periodogram stronger than white noise would produce?
tsm.fisher_g.h0: H0: the series is white noise (no periodicity).
tsm.fisher_g.yes: A periodic component stands out from noise.
tsm.fisher_g.no: No cycle stands out from noise.
tsm.seasonal_acf.what: Correlation between each value and the value one cycle earlier.
tsm.seasonal_acf.h0: H0: no correlation one cycle apart.
tsm.seasonal_acf.yes: Values are linked one cycle apart.
module.timeseries.label: Time series
ts.title: Time series
ts.description: One series, analysed in depth: overview and trend, seasonality, decomposition. Every section starts with its conclusion; pick any method you want to see.
ts.section.overview.question: How does the series evolve, and is there a trend?
ts.section.seasonality.question: Does the series repeat a pattern (by weekday, month, quarter…)?
ts.section.decomposition.question: How much of the variation is trend, how much is seasonality, and what is left?
ts.partial: The first or last {period} is incomplete: it is drawn but left out of the trend methods.
ts.profile.above: {label} is {pct} % above average once the trend is removed.
ts.profile.below: {label} is {pct} % below average once the trend is removed.
ts.overlayHint: The latest year in color: compare it with the previous ones at the same time of year.
ts.detrended: Seasons are compared once the trend is removed ({how}).
ts.filled: {count} empty periods were interpolated for these methods.
tsm.adf.what: Regresses each change on the previous level: a level that pulls changes back means the series returns to its mean.
tsm.kpss.what: Checks whether the deviations from the level (or trend) wander off. The reverse question of ADF.
tsm.phillips_perron.what: Dickey-Fuller corrected for autocorrelation and changing variance by a long-run variance, instead of extra lags.
tsm.df_gls.what: Removes the mean by GLS before a Dickey-Fuller test: more powerful than ADF when the series is close to a unit root.
tsm.zivot_andrews.what: A unit-root test that allows one structural break at an unknown date, so a single jump is not mistaken for a unit root.
tsm.zivot_andrews.h0: H0: unit root, without a break.
tsm.zivot_andrews.no: Cannot reject a unit root, even allowing a break.
tsm.variance_ratio.what: For a random walk, the variance of 4-period changes is 4 times that of 1-period changes. Robust to changing variance.
tsm.rur.what: Counts how often the series sets new records: a non-parametric test, robust to outliers and non-normal errors.
tsm.ljung_box.what: Tests all autocorrelations up to a lag at once (lag 1, one cycle, two cycles).
tsm.ljung_box.h0: H0: no autocorrelation up to the lag.
tsm.ljung_box.yes: Values are linked to past values.
tsm.ljung_box.no: No autocorrelation up to the lags tested.
tsm.durbin_watson.what: First-order autocorrelation of the residuals around a straight-line trend: about 2 means none, below 1.5 positive, above 2.5 negative.
tsm.box_pierce.what: The original version of Ljung–Box (less accurate on short series).
tsm.box_pierce.h0: H0: no autocorrelation up to the lag.
tsm.box_pierce.yes: Values are linked to past values.
tsm.box_pierce.no: No autocorrelation up to the lags tested.
tsm.breusch_godfrey.what: Regresses the residuals of a trend on their own past values (several lags at once).
tsm.breusch_godfrey.h0: H0: no autocorrelation of the residuals.
tsm.runs.what: Counts runs above and below the median: too few runs means values cluster.
tsm.turning_points.what: Counts peaks and troughs: a random series has about two thirds of its points as turning points.
tsm.turning_points.yes: Too few or too many turning points for a random order.
tsm.bartels.what: von Neumann's ratio on ranks: about 2 for a random order, lower when values persist.
ts.section.stationarity.question: Does the series keep a stable level and spread, or does it drift? (Most models need a stationary series.)
ts.section.autocorrelation.question: Do past values help predict the next ones?
ts.aroundTrend: tested around a trend (the trend is strong)
ts.stationarity.stationary: Stationary: ADF rejects a unit root and KPSS does not reject stationarity.
ts.stationarity.unit_root: Not stationary: ADF and KPSS agree on a unit root.
ts.stationarity.trend_or_difference: ADF and KPSS both reject: likely stationary around a trend or after differencing.
ts.stationarity.inconclusive: Inconclusive: neither ADF nor KPSS rejects. The evidence is weak either way (a strong cycle or a short series often causes this).
ts.memoryOn: Computed on the series transformed as chosen in Stationarity ({how}).
ts.acfHint: Correlation with the value k periods earlier; bars beyond the dotted lines are significant.
ts.pacfHint: The same, once the shorter lags are accounted for: where it stops points at the AR order.
ts.reading.slow_decay: The ACF decays slowly: a trend or a unit root. Try a difference.
ts.reading.seasonal_spikes: Spikes every cycle: seasonality to model or remove (seasonal difference).
ts.reading.pacf_cutoff: The PACF stops after lag {order}: an AR({order}) model is a good start.
ts.reading.white_noise: No autocorrelation beyond chance: the values behave like white noise.
tsm.breusch_pagan.what: Regresses the squared residuals on time: does the variance depend on time?
tsm.breusch_pagan.no: No evidence that the variance changes with time.
tsm.arch_lm.what: Are large shocks followed by large shocks? Regresses squared residuals on their own past.
tsm.arch_lm.yes: Volatility clusters: large shocks follow large shocks.
tsm.white.what: Like Breusch–Pagan, with time and time² (catches a variance that rises then falls).
tsm.white.no: No evidence that the variance changes.
tsm.goldfeld_quandt.what: Compares the variance of the first part with the last part (the middle 20 % left out).
tsm.goldfeld_quandt.h0: H0: same variance at the start and the end.
tsm.goldfeld_quandt.yes: The start and the end have different variances.
tsm.goldfeld_quandt.no: Same variance at the start and the end.
tsm.mcleod_li.what: Ljung–Box on the squared residuals: is the size of the shocks predictable?
tsm.mcleod_li.h0: H0: no autocorrelation of the squared residuals.
tsm.mcleod_li.yes: The size of the shocks is predictable (ARCH-like).
tsm.mcleod_li.no: The size of the shocks is not predictable.
tsm.levene.what: Compares the spread of 4 equal time windows (deviations from the mean).
tsm.brown_forsythe.what: Levene around the median: robust to skewed residuals.
tsm.bartlett.what: Compares the variances of 4 time windows; powerful but assumes normal residuals.
tsm.fligner.what: Rank-based comparison of spreads across windows: the most robust to outliers.
tsm.pettitt.what: Rank test for a single change of level at an unknown date.
tsm.pettitt.yes: A change of level is likely.
tsm.cusum.what: Cumulated deviations from the mean: drift beyond the bounds means the level is not stable.
tsm.cusum.yes: The level is not stable over time.
tsm.chow.what: F test of a different mean before and after one date (the strongest break found).
tsm.chow.h0: H0: same mean before and after.
tsm.chow.yes: The mean differs before and after.
tsm.buishand.what: Range of the cumulated deviations: large when the level shifts. p-value by simulation.
tsm.snht.what: Standard normal homogeneity test: the strongest split into two means. p-value by simulation.
ts.section.volatility.question: Does the variability change over time?
ts.section.residuals.question: What is left once trend and seasonality are removed, and how is it distributed?
ts.section.breaks.question: Does the series change regime, and which periods are atypical?
ts.volatility.on: Residuals ({how}) and their {window}-period rolling standard deviation.
ts.volatility.logHelps: The variability grows with the level: a log transformation usually stabilises it.
ts.residuals.about.returns: Relative change from one period to the next (value / previous − 1).
ts.residuals.skewness: 0 for a symmetric distribution; positive = a longer right tail.
ts.residuals.kurtosis: Excess kurtosis: 0 for a normal law; positive = heavier tails (more extreme values).
ts.residuals.qq: Quantiles against a normal law (points on the line = normal)
ts.breaks.deseasonalized: Searched on the series without its seasonality, so a regular cycle is not taken for a break.
ts.breaks.jumpUp: The level rises from {before} to {after} from {period}.
ts.breaks.jumpDown: The level falls from {before} to {after} from {period}.
ts.anomalies.none: No period stands out at this threshold.
ts.breaks.slope: The trend changes from {before} to {after} per {unit} from {period}.
tsm.naive.what: Every future period equals the last value: the simplest reference.
tsm.seasonal_naive.what: Every future period equals the same period of the last cycle: the reference for seasonal series.
tsm.ets_auto.what: Exponential smoothing: every admissible form of error, trend (damped or not) and seasonality, the lowest AICc kept.
tsm.arima_auto.what: Differences from the stationarity tests, then a stepwise search of the AR and MA orders (seasonal when the cycle is 24 periods or less) by AICc.
tsm.drift.what: A straight line from the first to the last value, extended.
tsm.mean.what: Every future period equals the average of the history.
tsm.ses.what: A weighted average where recent values count more; no trend, no seasonality.
tsm.holt.what: Exponential smoothing with a level and a trend.
tsm.holt_winters.what: Exponential smoothing with a level, a trend and an additive seasonality.
tsm.theta.what: Simple exponential smoothing with drift, on the deseasonalized series: a strong all-rounder in forecasting competitions.
tsm.sarima.what: ARIMA with the orders you set: (p,d,q) and seasonal (P,D,Q).
ts.section.forecast.question: What comes next, and which model forecasts this series best?
ts.forecast.idle: Forecasting fits several models several times; it starts when you click Run forecast.
ts.forecast.validation: Scored on {origins} rolling origins, each forecasting {horizon} periods it had not seen.
ts.forecast.residualsWhite: {model}: its residuals look like white noise (Ljung–Box) — the model captured the structure.
ts.forecast.residualsLinked: {model}: its residuals are still autocorrelated (Ljung–Box) — some structure is left; intervals may be too narrow.
ts.forecast.maseHint: Mean absolute error scaled by the naive reference's error: below 1 beats it.
ts.forecast.reading: Lower MASE, MAE and RMSE are better. Coverage should be close to the interval level (80 %, 95 %): far below means the intervals are too narrow. Click a model to draw it.
module.ml.label: Machine learning
ml.title: Machine learning
ml.description: Pick what to predict: the problem is recognised, the data prepared by explicit rules, and a first model trained at once. Change the settings, train again, compare.
ml.question: What do you want to predict?
ml.questionHint: Choose a column. Everything else has a default, explained on the left: you can train again with other settings afterwards.
ml.taskLong.binary: Binary classification — predicts one of two classes.
ml.taskLong.multiclass: Multiclass classification — predicts one of several classes.
ml.preparationAuto: Decided by rules from each column's type and the model; shown after the first training.
ml.validation: Validation: 80 / 20 split (stratified for classes), seed 42 · at most 200,000 training rows.
ml.verdict.regression: The model explains {r2} of the variation in {target} — {skill} better than always predicting the average.
ml.verdict.noBetterAverage: The model does no better than always predicting the average {target}: the features may not carry information about it.
ml.verdict.classification: Right {accuracy} of the time — always answering “{majority}” would be right {baseline}.
ml.verdict.noBetterMajority: The model does no better than always answering “{majority}”: the features may not carry information about the classes.
ml.rowsUsed: Trained on {train} rows, tested on {test} rows it had not seen
ml.explain.r2: Share of the variation explained, on the test rows: 1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the average.
ml.explain.mae: Mean absolute error, in the target's unit; “avg” is the error of always predicting the average.
ml.explain.rmse: Root mean squared error: like MAE but large errors weigh more.
ml.explain.skill: How much smaller the MAE is than the average's.
ml.explain.accuracy: Share of test rows classified right; “majority” is always answering the most frequent class.
ml.explain.balanced: Mean of the recall of each class: honest when classes are imbalanced.
ml.explain.f1: Mean over classes of the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
ml.explain.auc: Probability that a random positive row gets a higher score than a random negative one: 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect.
ml.explain.logloss: How confident and right the probabilities are: lower is better.
ml.predictedVsActual: Predicted against actual (on the line = perfect)
ml.heteroscedastic: The error grows or shrinks with the value (Breusch–Pagan {p}): predicting the log of the target often helps.
ml.homoscedastic: The error has a constant spread (Breusch–Pagan {p}).
ml.noCoefficients: This model has no coefficients to show.
ml.coefficientsHint: Effect of each prepared input on the prediction, other inputs held fixed. Inputs are standardised: compare their sizes; “per unit” turns a coefficient back into the column's own unit.
ml.coefficientsLogisticHint: Effect of each prepared input on the log-odds; the odds ratio is how the odds are multiplied when the input rises by one (standardised) unit.
ml.vifHint: Variance inflation factor: above 10, the input is largely explained by the others (unstable coefficient).
ml.predict.title: Use this model
ml.predict.noImport: Importing a model file is not offered here: a joblib file can run code when it is opened.
ml.predict.dialogHint: The data is checked against what the model was trained on before anything is predicted.
ml.predict.newFile: A new file? Import it from Home first, then pick it here.
ml.predict.keep: Columns to keep next to the predictions
ml.predict.targetPresent: This data has the answer: the predictions will be scored next to the validation.
ml.predict.sentenceLessReliable: {share} are less reliable: an important value the model never saw.
ml.predict.sentenceReliable: Every row looks like the training data.
ml.predict.lessReliableHint: Rows where an important column (5 % of the model's importance or more, or one of its 3 most important) has a category the model never saw or a value outside its training range.
ml.predict.intervalHint: Conformal: the half-width covers 90 % of the {errors} validation errors, so about 9 predictions in 10 fall within it.
ml.predict.distribution: Predictions on this data against the validation
ml.predict.scores: Scores on this data ({rows} rows with the answer)
ml.predict.holds: The model holds: its {metric} here is within 10 % of the validation's.
ml.predict.drops: The model does worse here: its {metric} is more than 10 % worse than the validation's.
ml.predict.rowsHint: Click a row to see why it got its prediction.
ml.predict.threshold: A row is “{positive}” when its probability is {threshold} or more (the run's threshold).
ml.verdict.overfit: With {inputs} inputs for {rows} training rows, it may be fitting noise: try Ridge regularization.
ts.anomalies.gesdAlpha: The generalized ESD test decides with its own significance level (α = 5 %)
ts.ar.title: Autoregressive model AR({order})
ts.ar.byAic: Order chosen by the lowest AIC (★ in the table).
ts.ar.residualsWhite: Its residuals look like white noise (Ljung–Box): this order captures the memory of the series.
ts.ar.residualsLinked: Its residuals are still autocorrelated (Ljung–Box): try a higher order, or a transformation.
tsm.tslm.what: A straight-line trend plus one indicator per position of the cycle, fitted by least squares, with exact prediction intervals.
tsm.gbm_lags.what: Trees predict each period from the previous ones (and the position in the cycle), on the series without its trend, one step at a time. Intervals are approximate.
tsm.mlp_lags.what: A small neural network predicts each period from the previous ones, on the series without its trend, one step at a time. Intervals are approximate.
tsm.croston.what: For series with many zeros: smooths the size of the non-zero values and the gap between them, separately. Forecast = size ÷ gap.
tsm.sba.what: Croston with the Syntetos–Boylan correction, which removes its tendency to forecast too high.
tsm.tsb.what: For series with many zeros: the chance of a non-zero value is updated every period, so the forecast falls when demand stops (end-of-life products).
tsm.adida.what: Sums the series over buckets as long as the usual gap between non-zero values, forecasts the sums, then spreads them back evenly.
tsm.combination.what: The average of the three models that validated best. Averaging is often more accurate than any single model; it is scored without hindsight.
lite.lockedBody: This version runs entirely in your browser: nothing is installed and your data never leaves this page. Some analyses are too heavy for it (machine learning, synthetic data, the assistant) and are kept for the app on your computer.
lite.lockedHow: Run the full app with one command (Windows, in PowerShell):
lite.loadingBody: Python and its scientific libraries start inside this page: about one to two minutes each time it opens, as nothing runs on a server. Your data never leaves your browser.
lite.failed: The analysis engine could not start: {error}
lite.methodLocked: Too slow in the browser: available in the full app.
ts.forecast.wapeHint: Total absolute error ÷ total actual value: the share of the volume that was missed. Works with zeros, unlike MAPE.
ts.demand.title: {pct} % of the periods are zero: {kind} demand.
ts.demand.detail: On average one non-zero value every {adi} periods (ADI), sizes varying by CV² = {cv2}. MAPE is not shown: it divides by zero.
ts.demand.suggest: Models built for this kind of series usually do better. Add them and run again.
ts.backtest.explain: Each colored line is a forecast {model} made at an earlier date, using only the periods before it; the grey line is what really happened. The scores in the table are the gaps between the two.
ts.ar.atBoundary: The AIC is still falling at the largest order tried ({order}): the series remembers further back — usually a cycle or a trend. Difference it (Stationarity) or model the season.
ml.prep.title: Preparation
ml.prep.appliesNext: Changes apply to the next training.
ml.prep.autoHint: Every choice comes from a named rule; change any of them below.
ml.prep.customHint: Your choices are marked with a dot; everything else stays automatic.
ml.prep.indicatorHint: Adds a 0 / 1 input that says the value was empty: emptiness is often informative.
ml.prep.leakConfirm: This column seems to contain the answer: the scores would look great and mean nothing. Use it anyway?
ml.prep.selectionHint: Optional: keep only some of the prepared inputs. Each checked method runs in order, fitted on the training rows only; the count shows what it kept.
ml.prep.methodWhat.correlation: Of two inputs correlated above the threshold, drops the second (default 0.95).
ml.prep.methodWhat.vif: Drops the most redundant input while its VIF exceeds the threshold (default 10).
ml.prep.methodWhat.mutual_info: Keeps the k inputs that tell the most about the target, linear or not (default 20).
ml.prep.methodWhat.univariate: Keeps inputs linked to the target on their own (F test, default p < 0.05).
ml.prep.methodWhat.l1: Keeps inputs a lasso keeps (strength by cross-validation; classification: C = 1).
ml.prep.methodWhat.rfe: Removes the weakest inputs step by step; the number kept is chosen by 3-fold cross-validation.
ml.prep.methodWhat.permutation: Keeps inputs whose shuffling hurts a quick model on held-out rows (default > 0).
ml.prep.numericImputeHint: Auto: mean if the column is nearly symmetric, median otherwise. KNN and iterative fill each value from the other columns.
ml.prep.indicatorShareHint: A column emptier than this gets a 0 / 1 “was missing” input.
ml.prep.rareHint: Categories under this share and this number of rows are grouped as Other.
ml.prep.oneHotLimitHint: Categories beyond this count use target encoding instead (linear models).
ml.prep.smoothingHint: Pulls rare categories towards the overall mean: higher = more cautious.
ml.prep.outliersHint: None by default: removing outliers often biases the model.
ml.prep.droppedRows: {count} training rows dropped (beyond 3 IQR); the test rows are untouched.
ml.prep.imbalanceHint: Applied to the training rows only: the test rows keep the real class shares, so the scores stay honest.
ml.prep.previewHint: The first training rows as the model receives them: {inputs} inputs, fitted on {rows} training rows.
ml.verdict.withinOne: {share} of predictions are right or off by one class.
ml.explain.withinOne: Classes are ordered: share of test rows predicted in the right class or the next one.
ml.classes.method.quantile: Equal counts — same number of rows in each class
ml.classes.method.width: Equal width — same range of {target} for each class
ml.classes.method.jenks: Natural breaks — limits where the data has gaps
ml.classes.ignoreOutliersHint: The width is computed between the 1st and 99th percentiles; the extremes go to the first and last classes.
ml.classes.histogram: Distribution of {target} with the class limits
ml.classes.name: Name of class {index}
ml.classes.small: {name} has only {count} rows — models will struggle to learn it.
ml.classes.ties: Many rows share the same values, so the classes are not exactly equal.
ml.classes.merged: Some limits fell on the same value: {count} classes instead of {wanted}.
ml.classes.estimated: Counts estimated on 0.1 % steps; the run gives the exact ones.
ml.classes.suggest: Few distinct values: predict them as classes?
ml.settings.title: Settings — {model}
ml.settings.description: Changes apply to the next training.
ml.settings.noOptimizer: This model has no optimizer settings.
ml.picker.title: Choose a model
ml.picker.count: {count} models for this problem, by family
ml.validation.methodHint.split: Train on a random share of the rows, test on the rest (stratified for classes).
ml.validation.methodHint.kfold: Every row is tested once by a model that did not see it; scores are the mean ± standard deviation over the folds, and the saved model is retrained on every row.
ml.validation.methodHint.repeated_kfold: k-fold repeated with different shuffles: steadier scores, k × repeats trainings.
ml.validation.methodHint.group_kfold: Rows of the same group (a customer, a store) are never on both sides.
ml.validation.methodHint.time_split: Test on the most recent rows: no test row is earlier than a training row.
ml.validation.methodHint.loo: One training per row (1,000 rows at most).
ml.validation.groupHint: Rows sharing a value of this column stay together.
ml.validation.metricHintRegression: Used for the run list and its ★.
ml.validation.metricHintClasses: Used for the run list and its ★; balanced accuracy suits imbalanced classes.
ml.rows.hint: Beyond the limit, a reproducible sample of the rows is used.
ml.crossValidated: {method}: every row predicted by a model that had not seen it; the saved model is retrained on every row.
ml.importancesHint: Share of the model's gain (or impurity reduction) due to each prepared input: big = used a lot, not necessarily causal. Permutation importance and SHAP come with explainability.
ml.explain.computing: Computing the explanation… (once per run, then kept)
ml.explain.failed: The explanation could not be computed.
ml.explain.permutationHint: How much the {metric} drops when one column is shuffled on {rows} evaluation rows (mean ± sd over 5 repeats): the column's real contribution to the score. Around 0 = the model does without it.
ml.explain.pair: {first} and {second} are strongly linked ({measure} = {strength}): their importance is shared between them.
ml.explain.shap: How each column moves the predictions (SHAP)
ml.explain.shapHint: One point per row ({rows} rows), one line per column: right of 0 pushes the prediction up, left pulls it down; color = the column's value (low → high). {method}, on the {scale} scale.
ml.explain.shapPositive: Two classes: contributions are in log-odds of “{positive}”.
ml.explain.dependenceHint: The average prediction when this column takes each value, every other column as it is; below, how many rows have each value (trust the curve where there are rows).
ml.explain.treeHint: A decision tree is its own explanation: each row follows the questions down to a leaf (4 levels shown).
ml.explain.rowSentence: Row {row}: the strongest pushes come from {columns}.
ml.explain.rowMissing: This row is not among the explained rows.
ml.errors.computing: Looking for where the model is wrong…
ml.errors.summary: On {rows} {source} · {label}: {overall} on average · {tested} subgroups tested in {columns} columns
ml.errors.slices: Subgroups where the model is wrong
ml.errors.slicesHint: Searched among every category and fifth of the columns that matter most, their pairs, and a shallow tree fitted on the error. Each subgroup is tested against the other rows, with false discoveries held at 5 % (Benjamini–Hochberg). The costliest first (rows × extra error). Click one for its rows.
ml.errors.ratioHint: Its error divided by the average error
ml.errors.allRows: Both pages show every row of the group, training rows included.
ml.errors.hintsHint: Simple, careful rules. The app applies none of them itself.
ml.errors.byColumnHint: Mean {label} per category or fifth of each column (dashed line: the average), the columns where it varies most first. Muted bars have fewer than 30 rows.
ml.errors.worstHint: The {count} held-out rows predicted worst. Click a row for its explanation.
ml.errors.groupsHint: Choose a sensitive column (sex, age…) to see the model's metrics for each of its groups side by side.
ml.errors.displayOnly: Display only: nothing is corrected. Groups under 30 rows (muted) are left out of the gap.
ml.errors.compareSummary: {label} on the {rows} held-out rows both runs predicted: {a} for {first}, {b} for {second}.
ml.compare.title: Compare models
ml.compare.description: Each checked model is trained with its defaults on the same rows, validation and preparation, one after the other.
ml.compare.finished: Done: best first. Each model is now a run you can open.
ml.runCompare.title: Runs side by side
ml.runCompare.pickHint: Tick two runs or more to compare them
ml.runCompare.otherValidation: Another validation (method, test size, folds, seed or rows): not comparable
ml.runCompare.differ: Highlighted rows: settings that differ between the runs.
ml.tune.nothing: This model has nothing worth tuning.
ml.tune.title: Tune — {model}
ml.tune.description: Searches the best settings with 3-fold cross-validation on the training rows only; the test rows judge the result once, when you use it.
ml.tune.spaceHint: Change a bound, the scale, or fix a setting to keep it out of the search. Bounds stay within what the model accepts.
ml.tune.preparing: Preparing the rows and judging the defaults…
ml.tune.importance: What mattered most in the search
ml.tune.useHint: Using them trains a new run, judged on the test rows.
ml.auto.buttonHint: Find the best model within a time budget
ml.auto.title: Auto — the best model in a time budget
ml.auto.description: Baselines, one model per family, the weakest stopped early, the 3 best tuned, then an ensemble kept only if it is clearly better. Every model is judged on the same folds.
ml.auto.stacking: Also try a linear stack of the best models
ml.auto.split: Your validation is a train / test split: the models are compared on 5 folds of the training rows, and the test rows only judge the model kept.
ml.auto.stepHint.baselines: A constant and the linear model: where we start from.
ml.auto.stepHint.families: One model per family with its defaults, cheapest first; those too slow for the budget are skipped.
ml.auto.stepHint.reduction: The weakest stop early, on fewer rows; the 3 best go on.
ml.auto.stepHint.tuning: Optuna on the 3 best families, the time left shared by rank.
ml.auto.stepHint.ensemble: Greedy selection on out-of-fold predictions, kept only if clearly better.
ml.auto.stoppedTitle: Stopped: the best model so far is saved as a run
ml.auto.failedTitle: The Auto could not keep a model
ml.estimate.result: About {duration} ({fits}), from fits on 500 and 2,000 rows.
ml.validation.thresholdHint: Chosen on out-of-fold predictions of the training rows, then applied once to the test rows.
ml.validation.methodHint.panel_walk_forw: Periods in order: each fold trains on earlier periods, leaves the embargo out, then is tested on the next block. Every test period is scored on its own.
ml.validation.periodHint: A date or a growing number (era, month) whose values come back on many rows. Left out of the features.
ml.validation.entityHint: An id seen at every period (optional). Left out of the features; used for the leak checks and the embargo.
ml.validation.embargoHint: Periods left out between training and each test block.
ml.validation.windowPeriodsHint: Empty: as many as the first fold trains on.
ml.validation.samplePeriodsHint: Whole periods only, never rows drawn inside a period.
ml.validation.criterionHint: Ranks the runs, Compare models and Tune. Mean / std rewards a steady model.
ml.rows.panelHint: On a panel, a sample keeps whole periods (one in k, counting back from the most recent).
ml.panel.duplicates: {count} rows repeat an ({entity}, {period}) pair: a random split puts copies on both sides.
ml.panel.bothSides: With this validation the same {entities} are in training and test rows: the score carries what the model learnt about each of them.
ml.periods.verdict: {metric} per {period}: {mean} on average over {count} test periods, with a spread of {std}; the worst is {worst} ({worstPeriod}).
ml.periods.explain.mean: The metric computed on each test period, then averaged.
ml.periods.explain.sharpe: The mean score divided by its spread over the periods: how steady the model is (the Sharpe ratio of the scores).
ml.periods.explain.good: Share of the test periods on the right side of the threshold: 0 for a correlation or R², 0.5 for an AUC.
ml.periods.criterion: The run's score: {criterion} over the periods.
ml.periods.foldsHint: Window {window} · embargo {embargo} · trained on 1 period in {step}.
ml.periods.noAlert: No panel leak found: no column from the future, no suspicious score.
ml.exposure.title: Dependence on single columns
ml.exposure.hint: Correlation of the predictions with each number column, period by period, averaged over the periods. A model that follows one column closely is only as good as that column.
ml.exposure.none: Exposure is measured for numbers and two classes.
ml.neutralize.title: Neutralize
ml.neutralize.hint: Remove from the predictions the part these columns explain linearly, period by period, then score every period again. A steadier model can be worth more than a stronger one on average.
ml.neutralize.result: After neutralizing: {metric} {mean} on average (was {before}), mean / std {sharpe} (was {sharpeBefore}).
ml.thresholdChosen: Decision threshold {threshold} ({rule}, chosen on the training rows): the predicted classes and the scores use it.
ts.anomalies.strongest: The {shown} strongest of {count}, strongest first; every one is marked on the chart.
module.kpi.label: KPI
kpi.title: KPI builder
kpi.description: A business indicator in one click: the measure, grain, chart and table are chosen for you. Customise anything afterwards.
kpi.savedEmpty: None yet: save the one you see.
kpi.ratioNeedsTwo: Add a second measure first: a ratio divides one measure by another.
kpi.noDate: No date column — values over the whole data
kpi.noSplit: No category column to split by
kpi.lineWhy: A line through the bars; when the bars are split, one line per category, in its colour.
kpi.shareLabel: Add a “% of total” chart below
kpi.valueLabels.auto: Auto: on up to 12 bars, else the last value of up to 4 lines
kpi.top.auto: Auto: the 8 largest, the rest grouped as Other
kpi.groupsNeedCalculate: Top N and the order change the numbers: click Calculate.
kpi.format.name: Display name
kpi.partialNote: † Incomplete period: left out of the tiles and of the changes.
kpi.hiddenOther: “Other” is hidden; the totals still include it.
kpi.measure.hint: What to count or add up
kpi.pending: Changes not applied yet: click Calculate.
ml.classCurves: Each class against all the others (one-vs-rest): the further a curve bows to the top left, the better the model tells that class apart.
kpi.pageFilters.help: Unticked, the KPI ignores the filters set at the top of the page.
module.synthetic.label: Synthetic data
settings.computeIntro: The graphics card the deep synthetic-data models (CTGAN, TVAE, TimeGAN) will use. They come next: today the setting is saved but has no effect.
settings.useGpuHint: Used by the deep models (CTGAN, TVAE, TimeGAN), coming next.
settings.useGpuNone: No ready GPU: the deep models will run on the CPU.
synthetic.title: Synthetic data
synthetic.description: Generate an artificial copy of the data that keeps its distributions and links without copying its rows, then see how faithful it is and how well it protects the real rows.
synthetic.notReady: The dataset is not ready yet.
synthetic.dropCopies: Drop copies of unique real rows
synthetic.dropCopiesHint: Synthetic rows identical to a real row that is unique in the data are replaced by spare generated rows.
synthetic.learnsFrom: learns from {rows} rows; 20 % of the real rows are held out to check privacy
synthetic.deleteConfirm: Delete this {method} run and its synthetic data?
synthetic.empty: Ready: every choice above is automatic. Click Generate.
synthetic.diagnosticHelp: Validity checks (SDMetrics' Diagnostic): values inside the real bounds, only existing levels, unique identifiers, whole numbers, the planned columns. Expected: 100 %.
synthetic.qualityHelp: Resemblance, computed as SDMetrics' Quality score: the mean of Column shapes (KS / TV complements) and Column pair trends (only pairs strongly linked in the real data count).
synthetic.detectionHelp: Can a classifier tell real from synthetic rows? 1 − (2 × AUC − 1), the stricter of logistic regression and gradient boosting. 100 % = indistinguishable. A measure of fidelity, not of privacy.
synthetic.privacyHelp: The lower of: share of synthetic rows that copy no real row, and protection against memorisation (synthetic rows are no closer to the training rows than to new real rows).
synthetic.histogramOf: {column}: real and synthetic on the same intervals
synthetic.linksHelp: r between numbers, Cramér's V between categories, η between a number and a category. Click a cell to open the pair.
synthetic.noPairs: Needs at least two modelled columns.
synthetic.coverage: Coverage and empty values (beside the score)
synthetic.coverageHelp: Low coverage means a generator that collapses onto the most frequent values: tails, rare levels or outliers lost.
synthetic.trendsHelp: Only pairs strongly linked in the real data count in the score (|r| > 0.5 or Cramér's V > 0.3), as SDMetrics does.
synthetic.pcaHelp: Two components fitted on the real data; synthetic rows projected in the same plane should cover the same cloud.
synthetic.nothingLeftOut: Every column is in the synthetic data.
synthetic.privacyMeasures: Measures (against real rows the generator never saw)
synthetic.exactCopiesHelp: Synthetic rows identical to any real row. A combination many real rows share (same category, same small number) reveals nobody.
synthetic.nearCopiesHelp: Numbers within 1 % of the range (SDMetrics). Naturally higher on data with few columns.
synthetic.overfittingHelp: {share} of synthetic rows are closer to the training rows than to new real rows (50 % expected). Under 80 %: memorisation.
synthetic.baselineHelp: Median distance to the closest real row ({median}) against random rows. Low is not a defect by itself: faithful data is close to the real data.
synthetic.dcr: Distance to the closest training row
synthetic.dcrHelp: Synthetic rows should be no closer to the training rows than new real rows are.
synthetic.noRare: No level seen fewer than 5 times appears in the synthetic data.
synthetic.rareHelp: A level seen fewer than 5 times can point to a person.
synthetic.capHelp: Knowing some columns of a real person (age, postcode…), how often do the matching synthetic rows reveal a sensitive one? Compared with a random guess.
synthetic.notDifferential: Synthetic data is not a differential-privacy guarantee: read these measures together.
synthetic.utilityHelp: Two identical models predict the chosen column: one trained on the real training rows, one on the synthetic rows. Both are tested on the same real rows held out from the generator.
synthetic.utilityResult: Predicting {target}, tested on {rows} held-out real rows
synthetic.utilityRows: {train} real and {synthetic} synthetic training rows; {test} test rows.
synthetic.deviceToggle: Train this run on the GPU or the CPU
synthetic.noGpu: No GPU ready (or Use the GPU is off in Settings): trains on the CPU
synthetic.uniqueCopiesHelp: Synthetic rows identical to a real row that no other real row shares: they can point to a person. Expected: 0.
synthetic.autocorrelationHelp: 1 − mean gap between the real and synthetic autocorrelations (lags 1 to 10): how alike the dynamics are.
synthetic.discriminativeHelp: A recurrent classifier tries to tell real from synthetic windows; 100 % = it cannot.
synthetic.predictiveHelp: Next-step error trained on real ({real}) vs on synthetic ({synthetic}) windows, tested on held-out real histories.
synthetic.sequencesOf: {sequences} synthetic sequences of {length} steps ({step}); entity: {entity}; learned from {windows} real windows.
report.hint: One HTML file about the whole dataset, after your filters: summary, every variable, correlations, missing values.
agent.title: Assistant
agent.intro: Ask about this dataset: the assistant runs the app's analyses, reads their results and explains them. Every figure it gives comes from an analysis you can open.
agent.suggest.overview: What stands out in this dataset?
agent.suggest.quality: Which columns need cleaning before an analysis?
agent.suggest.drivers: What is most linked to {column}, and how?
agent.suggest.links: Which columns are most strongly linked?
agent.setupKey: The assistant works with your own API key: Anthropic (Claude), Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, or a local model. Add it in the settings; it stays on this computer.
agent.sdkMissing: The assistant needs the AI SDKs, which are not installed: run `uv sync --extra agent` in backend/, then restart the app.
agent.privacy: What leaves this computer: your messages, the column names and types, and the statistics the analyses return (counts, means, tests, the most frequent values). Never whole rows.
agent.keyNone: No key yet. Create one on {console}.
agent.effortHint: How hard the model thinks before acting: higher is more thorough, slower and more expensive.
agent.budgetHint: The assistant stops when a conversation reaches it; raise it to go on.
agent.placeholderDisabled: Add an API key in the settings first
agent.costHint: Estimated from the tokens each answer used
agent.confirmTitle: The assistant asks before changing something
agent.providerHint: Automatic uses the first provider with a key. Pasting a key from Anthropic, Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter or Groq switches to that provider by itself.
agent.keyOptional: A local server usually needs no key.
agent.tokenBudget: Prices are only known for Claude models: with this provider, each conversation stops at {limit} tokens.
agent.tokensHint: Tokens used by this conversation (price unknown for this model)
agent.unverifiedOne: 1 figure not found in the analyses: {figures}
agent.unverifiedMany: {count} figures not found in the analyses: {figures}
agent.unverifiedHint: Every figure should come from an analysis the assistant ran. These ones could not be matched: they may be computed by the model (a difference, a ratio) or wrong. Check them before relying on them.
agent.notesIntro: Facts every conversation on this dataset starts with: the target, units, what a code means, a known problem. The assistant can add one when you confirm it.
changes.title: Changes
changes.description: What changed since the previous version of this file, or against another dataset: columns, quality, distributions, rows, KPIs and relations. Check it before trusting the numbers.
changes.noPreviousHint: The app keeps a statistical photo of every import. Reimport this dataset once its source has changed, or pick another dataset to compare with (above, or tick two datasets on the home page).
changes.quality.dates: Dates out of the usual range
changes.quality.hint: Unusual = beyond 1.5 IQR of each version's quartiles, as on the variable page.
changes.distributions.none: No column to compare: numbers, categories and dates are compared.
changes.distributions.title: Strongest shift first
changes.psiHelp: Population stability index: how far the shares moved, on the old version's deciles (numbers) or values (categories). Below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate, above 0.25 strong. Ranked by this effect size, not by p-value: on a million rows every difference is significant.
changes.distanceHelp: Wasserstein distance between the two distributions, in units of the old interquartile range: 0.5 IQR means values moved by half the spread of the middle of the data.
changes.longTailHelp: Most rows hold a value outside the 50 most frequent (invoices, customers): new values are expected, so this column is not counted as shifted.
changes.periodsLabel: Rows per period of {column}, before and after
changes.uncertainHint: The other version only kept its 50 most frequent values: this one may have been there, rarer.
changes.rows.examplesHint: The first 100 changed values; the CSV holds them all.
changes.kpis.none: No saved KPI on this dataset.
changes.kpis.name: KPI
changes.kpis.hint: A past period present in both versions whose value changed points at a correction made back in the source.
changes.kpis.broken: Can't be computed on this version
changes.kpis.unavailable: Not available for the previous version
changes.relations.hint: The 10 strongest relations of each version (Correlations page), with their value in the other.
changes.pickTwo: Tick two datasets to compare them
changes.pickOneMore: Tick one more dataset to compare
settings.keepVersionHint: At a reimport, the previous rows are kept for the row by row comparison (statistics are always kept). Kept now: {size}.
module.experiments.label: Experiments
experiments.title: Experiments
experiments.description: Did variant B do better than A, and is it more than chance? Describe the test once: the right test, intervals, Holm-adjusted p-values and the power are chosen and explained for you. Plan the next one with the sample size.
experiments.noCandidates: No column can describe an experiment here: it needs a column with 2 to 5 variants and a number or yes/no column to compare.
experiments.cupedHint: CUPED: the same measure before the test (last month's spend) narrows the interval without biasing it. A ratio divides two sums per unit (revenue ÷ orders).
experiments.intervalsLabel: Difference of {metric} to the control, with its interval
experiments.reference: Reference: every difference is against the control.
experiments.test.z_proportions: z-test of two proportions: are the two rates further apart than chance would make them? The interval of the difference is Newcomb's (hybrid Wilson), reliable even for rates near 0 or 1.
experiments.test.welch_t: Welch's t-test compares two means without assuming equal variances. With thousands of units it holds even for skewed values; when they are very skewed, Mann–Whitney and a bootstrap interval are shown as checks.
experiments.test.poisson: Counts whose variance is close to their mean behave like Poisson counts: the rates per unit are compared with a score test. When the variance is much larger, Welch's t is used instead.
experiments.test.delta_ratio: A ratio of sums (revenue ÷ orders) is computed per unit, so a heavy buyer counts once; its standard error comes from the delta method, and a bootstrap that resamples whole units checks it.
experiments.explain.cuped: CUPED subtracts what the pre-period measure predicts of each unit's value. The assignment is random, so the difference stays unbiased; only the noise shrinks, by about the square of the correlation.
experiments.explain.interval: The 95 % interval is the range of differences compatible with the data. If it excludes 0, the difference is significant at 5 %. The lift is the difference divided by the control's value.
experiments.explain.power: Power: the chance this sample had to detect the observed difference. Detectable lift: the smallest lift these groups detect 80 % of the time. Not significant with low power means not enough data, not “no effect”.
experiments.explain.holm: Several variants or metrics mean several chances of a false alarm: Holm's correction adjusts every p-value for the number of comparisons (less strict than Bonferroni, same guarantee).
experiments.cumulativeLabel: Cumulative difference of {metric} to the control over time
experiments.plan.intro: Before running a test: how many units each group needs to detect the effect you care about, and how long that takes at your traffic.
experiments.plan.liftUnit: The effect is a relative lift: 5 means +5 % of the current value.
experiments.plan.pointsUnit: The effect is in percentage points: 1 means 10 % → 11 %.
experiments.plan.incomplete: Give the current value and the effect to detect (and the standard deviation of a mean).
experiments.plan.curveTitle: Units per group and the smallest lift they detect
experiments.plan.curveLabel: Units per group against the smallest detectable lift
experiments.plan.curveNote: Halving the effect to detect needs about four times the units.
module.segments.label: Segments
segments.title: Segments
segments.description: Groups of similar rows, found and described for you, and rows unlike the others. The app picks the columns, prepares them and chooses how many segments hold up.
segments.first: Finding segments with the app's choices…
segments.runCompare.hint: Tick 2 to 5 runs to compare them
segments.sampledNote: Fitted on a reproducible sample of {rows} rows; every other row went to its nearest segment.
segments.scoresHelp: Each k from 2 to 10 is tried. Silhouette: how much closer rows are to their own segment than to the next one (−1 to 1). Calinski–Harabasz: spread between segments over spread within. Davies–Bouldin: how much segments overlap (lower is better). Inertia: spread within segments; the elbow is where adding a segment stops helping. The dotted line is the k kept.
segments.notGrouped: Rows HDBSCAN did not place in any group: too far from every dense region.
segments.mapPcaHelp: The prepared rows projected on their two principal components; the share of the variance each one explains is in the axis title. Diamonds are the segments' centres.
segments.mapTsneHelp: t-SNE keeps neighbours together; the distances between groups and their sizes do not mean much.
segments.profilesHelp: One line per column: the mean (numbers) or the most frequent category with its share. Highlighted cells differ strongly from the whole (standardised gap of 0.8 or more).
segments.profilesNote: In the columns' own units, on the rows the segments were fitted on.
segments.stabilityHelp: The same method is refitted on 10 subsamples of 80 % of the rows and compared with these segments (adjusted Rand index: 1 = the same groups, 0 = no better than chance). Below 0.6 the segments are not stable.
segments.dendrogramNote: Ward's tree on {rows} rows, cut (dashed line) where the segments are.
segments.saveHint: A new dataset with the same rows (filtered as they were) and a segment column; it opens in Compare, KPI, ML and Time series. The source is not changed.
segments.agreementHelp: Agreement: adjusted Rand index between two runs' segments, on the rows they share (1 = the same groups).
segments.columnsHint: The ML preparation rules with the distance profile: every number scaled robustly, categories one-hot (20 at most). Changes apply to both sections.
unusual.methodHelp.auto: Robust Mahalanobis on a few roughly elliptical numbers, Isolation Forest otherwise.
unusual.methodHelp.isolation_forest: 200 trees cut the rows apart; unusual rows are isolated in few cuts.
unusual.methodHelp.mahalanobis: Distance from the centre, taking correlations into account, with a robust covariance (MCD). Numbers only.
unusual.methodHelp.lof: Rows isolated in their own neighbourhood, even if normal elsewhere.
unusual.segmentFrom: Measured from the latest segmentation ({run} segments).
unusual.columnsAuto: Same columns and preparation as Segments (automatic).
unusual.columnsCustom: Same columns and preparation as Segments (your choices).
unusual.first: Looking for unusual rows with the app's choices…
unusual.headline: {rows} unusual rows of {of}
unusual.sampled: Fitted on a reproducible sample of {rows} rows; every row was scored.
unusual.curveHelp: Each row's score, sorted. The proposed threshold sits where the curve breaks (steep, then flat), else at the 1 % most unusual rows. Move it with the slider or click the curve: the rows follow without scoring again.
unusual.listedNote: The {rows} most unusual rows are listed with their reasons; the threshold moves among them.
unusual.percentile: {share} % of rows are at or below (median {median})
tsm.sarimax.what: The automatic ARIMA's orders, found without drivers, then refitted with the drivers as regressors (regression with ARIMA errors). Without drivers it is the automatic ARIMA.
ts.drivers.title: Drivers
ts.drivers.usedBy: Used by SARIMAX, Linear regression and Gradient boosting; the other models ignore them.
ts.drivers.explain: Outside variables that may explain the series, summed or averaged per period like it (a yes/no column becomes the share of rows that are yes). Known in advance: you give their future values. Past only: they enter lagged by the horizon, so nothing from the future leaks in.
ts.drivers.lagged: Enters lagged by {lag} periods (the horizon): no future value needed.
ts.drivers.lastWarn: The last value is repeated: this assumes it stays flat.
ts.drivers.flagHint: 0/1 flag, known in advance: future rows of the file, 0 where there is none.
ts.drivers.none: No other numeric or yes/no column to use.
ts.drivers.noModel: None of the chosen models uses drivers.
ts.drivers.suggest: {what} and {name} move together (r = {r} between their changes): use {name} as a driver.
ts.drivers.resultsHint: Each driver model was scored again without each driver, on the same rolling origins. A driver helps when the MASE is at least 5 % lower with it; within 5 % the gain is unclear.
ts.groups.title: Every group
ts.groups.countLimited: {n} {group} values · the {limit} largest on their own
ts.groups.global: Global model (one gradient boosting over every series)
ts.groups.notSummable: Totals only add up for sums and counts: choose Sum or Count to reconcile.
ts.groups.browser: Browser version: at most {n} series, forecast one after the other.
ts.groups.progress: Progress of the forecast of every group
ts.groups.stage.global: Training the global model on every series…
ts.groups.idle: Forecasts the {n} {group} series one by one, each scored on its own rolling origins; the best model is kept per series.
ts.groups.noneScored: No series could be scored: the histories are too short to validate.
ts.groups.globalWins: The global model wins for {wins} of {series}.
ts.groups.bestModels: Best model, by number of series
ts.groups.coherent: Every parent equals the sum of its children at every date (largest gap {gap}).
ts.groups.largest: The {n} largest {group} values: history and forecast with its 95 % band
ts.groups.exportHint: Long format: one line per series and period, with the 80 % and 95 % bounds.
ts.scenario.title: Scenarios
ts.scenario.explain: What if a driver known in advance changed? Up to 3 named scenarios, kept in the page's link.
ts.scenario.needsKnown: Scenarios need a driver known in advance (price, promotion, budget).
ts.scenario.name: Scenario
